analysis.one_liner: Blocks companies that spill oil into US waters from deducting the cleanup and liability costs from their taxes.
analysis.headline: A bill to stop oil companies from deducting oil-spill costs from their taxes died in the Senate Finance Committee without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: After an oil spill, the company responsible currently writes off its cleanup and liability payments as a business expense, which lowers its tax bill — meaning taxpayers effectively help cover the cost of disasters like Deepwater Horizon. This bill would have changed the tax code so those payments could no longer be deducted, making the polluter bear the full after-tax cost. It never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers generally, since spill costs would no longer be partially financed through the federal tax code, and coastal communities whose waters and economies suffer when a polluter can write off part of the damage it causes. Tax revenues would rise modestly, reducing pressure on other taxpayers.

how_it_helps.text: By denying the deduction, the bill would make oil-spill costs fully count against the polluter's income, ending a subsidy in which the tax code partially reimburses companies for the damage they cause.
It applies prospectively to tax returns due after enactment, so it would govern future spill liability, including incidents like Deepwater Horizon-style disasters in Gulf waters.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies that cause spills, which would bear the full after-tax cost of cleanup and liability payments instead of shifting part of it to the federal Treasury. Some of that cost could be passed to consumers through energy prices.

drawbacks.text: Removing the deduction raises the after-tax cost of responding to a spill, which the oil industry would characterize as increasing the cost of doing business and, ultimately, energy prices for consumers.

The deduction denial applies broadly to any responsible party for any oil discharge (except acts of God or war), not just major disasters, so even small-spill cleanup costs would become nondeductible.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real: companies that spill oil into public waters currently recover part of their cleanup and liability costs through the tax system, effectively making taxpayers co-fund the aftermath. The cost is modest and debatable: removing the deduction raises the company's after-tax cost of an accident, which could slightly increase energy prices, and cleanup outlays would still occur — they just would not be subsidized. The bill was one sentence long and narrow, so design risk was low. Its weakness was political, not substantive: it went nowhere.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and died there when the Congress ended, never getting a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Senator Bill Nelson of Florida introduced the bill on May 12, 2011, roughly a year after the Deepwater Horizon disaster polluted Gulf of Mexico waters off his state.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; that was the last action of any kind in the bill's history.
Three Democratic senators cosponsored the bill; no Republican did, and the Finance Committee never took it up before the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil companies kept the ability to deduct oil-spill costs from their taxes, leaving part of spill cleanup and liability effectively financed by taxpayers.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil companies keeping the spill deduction

for.name: Sen. Bill Nelson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill after the Deepwater Horizon spill affected Florida's Gulf coast.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: No Republican senator cosponsored the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all three cosponsors were Democrats; no Republicans signed on, and the Democratic-run Finance Committee also took no action.

industries.industry: Oil and gas companies (offshore drillers and shippers)
industries.note: They would lose a tax deduction that lets them write off cleanup and liability costs after a spill, raising the after-tax price of causing one. Today taxpayers effectively co-fund the cleanup through lost revenue.

Not an industry, but the fiscal and public interest: cleanup costs would no longer be partially financed through the federal tax code, and the full cost of a spill would stay on the party that caused it.
